title: The Richest Man Who Ever Lived Crashed a Country's Gold
titles: The Richest Man Who Ever Lived Crashed a Country's Gold
He Had So Much Gold, a Whole City Went Broke
The Richest Man in History Ran Out of Money
description: In 1324, Mansa Musa, the king of Mali and probably the richest man who ever lived, gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value fell for twelve years. This is the true story of his gold, his pilgrimage, the enslaved people the legend forgets, and the empire that fell after him.

summary_short.say: In 1324, a king from Mali walked into Cairo on his way to Mecca. His caravan carried so much gold that he gave it away to everyone. The Sultan, officials, the poor, the markets. Suddenly the whole city had gold. And its value fell. Twelve years later, a historian in Cairo wrote that it still had not recovered. Then, on the way home, the richest man who ever lived ran out of money and had to borrow it back. His name was Mansa Musa. The full story is on the channel.

facts_to_check: Mansa Musa ruled Mali from about 1312 (some say 1307) to about 1337
His pilgrimage to Mecca was in 1324-1325; he passed through Cairo in July 1324
Caravan size: chroniclers give tens of thousands of people (often quoted 60,000) and thousands of enslaved people; numbers likely exaggerated
Reports of camels carrying 50-300 pounds of gold each come from later accounts
al-Umari (writing c. 1337-38) reported the gold mithqal fell from above 25 to below 22 dirhams and had not recovered after 12 years
Musa borrowed from Cairo merchants on the way home (reported by al-Umari / Ibn Khaldun)
Musa told al-Umari about his predecessor's Atlantic voyage (2,000 ships); historians debate it
Abu Ishaq al-Sahili came back with Musa; Djinguereber Mosque, Timbuktu, c. 1327
Catalan Atlas (1375, Majorca, Abraham Cresques workshop) shows Musa holding a gold nugget
Songhai under Sunni Ali took Timbuktu in 1468; Tuareg had taken it around 1433
Portuguese built Elmina Castle on the Gold Coast in 1482
Ghana Empire, Wangara gold traders and the silent trade (al-Masudi / old accounts)
Sundiata Keita defeated Sumanguru at Kirina c. 1235; Musa from the Keita family
Kankan/Kanku Musa = his mother's name (Mande tradition)
Ibn Amir Hajib was Musa's host in Cairo and al-Umari's source
Gao taken by Musa's general (Sagmandia) c. 1325; scholars sent to Fez
Return trip losses: some accounts report many people and animals died
Maghan succeeded Musa; then Sulayman; Ibn Battuta in Mali 1352-53 (stingy gift, safe roads)
2012-13: militants in Timbuktu, mausoleums destroyed, 350,000+ manuscripts smuggled to Bamako, Ahmed Baba Institute fire Jan 2013
The $400 billion figure is a modern internet estimate (Celebrity Net Worth, 2012-2015 lists), not a historical calculation

scenes.say: In the summer of thirteen twenty four, a man walked into Cairo with so much gold that the price of gold in the city collapsed... and did not recover for twelve years.
He was not a conqueror on a raid. He was a pilgrim on his way to Mecca. And he was, by most accounts, the richest human being who ever lived.

Hi. Tonight's story sounds like a fairy tale. A king, a mountain of gold, a desert crossing. But every part of it was written down by people who were there... and the ending is darker than the legend.
His name was Musa. His people called him Mansa, which means king. And to understand how one man became richer than any emperor before or since, we have to start with dirt.
West Africa, seven hundred years ago. South of the Sahara, in the river valleys of Bambuk and Bure, the ground itself was full of gold.
Men dug it out of riverbanks and shallow pits, washed it, and carried it north in small leather bags. Not bars. Dust.
And in the north, across the desert, was the other half of the deal: salt. In the Sahara, salt was mined in slabs, and traders said a slab of salt could be worth its weight in gold.

The kings of Mali did not own every mine. They did something smarter. They controlled the roads. Every caravan, every bag of gold, every slab of salt passed through their cities, and the king took his share.
Think about that. He didn't need to dig. He just needed to be standing where everyone else had to walk.

Mali was not the first empire to grow rich this way. Before it came Ghana, an old kingdom in the same region. Arab writers called it the land of gold, and its kings were said to tie their horses to nuggets of gold.

Ghana's gold came from traders called the Wangara. They guarded the location of the mines so carefully that, according to old stories, outsiders traded with them without ever seeing their faces. Goods were left on the ground. Gold was left beside them. Nobody spoke.

lines: goods on the ground, gold beside them.

scenes.say: When Ghana weakened, a new power rose. In the twelve thirties, a prince named Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru and united the Mande peoples. That was the birth of the Mali Empire.
We know Sundiata mostly through the griots, the storytellers of West Africa, who have passed his epic from parent to child for nearly eight hundred years. Musa came from the same royal family.
Musa had another name too. Kankan Musa. In the Mande tradition, Kankan was his mother's name. Even the richest king in history was known as his mother's son.
By the time Musa came to power, around thirteen twelve, Mali stretched from the Atlantic coast deep into the desert. Bigger than Western Europe. Cities like Niani, Timbuktu and Gao paid him tribute.
But how Musa got the throne is one of the strangest stories in African history. And we only know it because Musa told it himself.
According to an Arab writer in Cairo, Musa said the king before him did not believe the ocean had an end. So he built a fleet... and sent it west, into the Atlantic.
Only one boat came back. Its captain said the others had been pulled away by a current, like a river in the middle of the sea.
So the king prepared two thousand more boats, took command himself, and sailed west. He never returned. Musa, who had been left in charge, became king.

visuals.label: the fleet Musa described
visuals.note: Musa's own account, recorded by al-Umari

scenes.say: Historians still argue whether that voyage really happened. But notice something. The richest man in history began his reign with a story about someone who risked everything... and lost it.
In thirteen twenty four, Musa decided to do what every devout Muslim hopes to do once in a lifetime. Make the pilgrimage to Mecca.
The journey was about four thousand miles. Across the Sahara, through Egypt, along the Red Sea. It took more than a year.
And he did not travel light. Writers of the time describe a caravan of tens of thousands of people. Soldiers, officials, servants... and thousands of enslaved men and women.
That part rarely makes it into the legend. The richest man in history crossed the desert with human beings he owned.

Some accounts say each enslaved servant carried a staff of gold. Dozens of camels carried gold dust, by some reports up to three hundred pounds each. The numbers are probably exaggerated. But everyone who saw it agreed on one thing. It was the most gold they had ever seen.

visuals.label: of gold per camel, in some reports

scenes.say: Crossing the Sahara was not a royal parade. It meant weeks between wells, sandstorms, freezing nights and burning days. Caravans followed routes that guides had memorized for generations. One wrong turn, and a whole caravan could die of thirst.
Along the way stood oasis towns like Walata and Taghaza. At Taghaza, travelers later wrote, even the houses and the mosque were built from blocks of salt.
Now look at this. This is how modern historians picture that caravan.
In July thirteen twenty four, the caravan reached Cairo. At the time, one of the biggest and richest cities in the world.
The Sultan of Egypt wanted Musa to kneel before him. Musa refused at first. In the end, he bowed... but said he was bowing to God, not to the Sultan.

And then he started giving. Gold to the Sultan. Gold to officials. Gold to the poor. Gold to anyone who asked. His people bought silk and slaves and goods in the markets and paid whatever price they were told.
Imagine you are a merchant in Cairo. Suddenly everyone has gold. So what happens to the value of gold?
It falls. Before Musa arrived, one measure of gold, a mithqal, was worth about twenty five silver dirhams. After he left, it was worth less than twenty two.

visuals.title: One mithqal of gold, in silver dirhams

scenes.say: How do we know any of this? Because of one man in Cairo. An official named Ibn Amir Hajib was assigned to look after the king of Mali. He became Musa's friend, talked with him for weeks, and later told everything to a historian.
Twelve years later, the historian al-Umari visited Cairo and asked about it. The people told him the price had still not recovered.

visuals.text: Gold was at a high price in Egypt until they came in that year... it has remained low until now.

scenes.say: One man, on one trip, crashed the value of gold in one of the richest cities on Earth. Economists today use his story to explain inflation.

From Cairo, Musa went on to Mecca and Medina and completed the pilgrimage. Reports say he gave generously there too, to the holy cities and the poor. For many Muslims who saw him, he was not a symbol of greed. He was a pious king from a land most of them had never seen.
And here is the twist nobody expects. On the way home, the richest man in the world... ran out of money.
He had given away and spent so much that he had to borrow from the merchants of Cairo. According to accounts of the time, at very high interest.

Some historians even think he borrowed partly to pull gold back out of the market and fix the damage he had done. If that is true, it may be one of the first attempts in history to control a currency.

The road home was cruel. Some accounts say the caravan lost many people and animals on the return across the desert. The legend counts the gold that arrived in Cairo. Nobody counted the people who never made it back.
Either way, the lesson was the same. Even the richest man alive could not spend money faster than it lost its value.
Musa did not come home with only memories. He came home with scholars, books, and an architect from Andalusia named Abu Ishaq al-Sahili.
In Timbuktu, a great mosque went up. Djinguereber. Made of mud and wood, it still stands today, almost seven hundred years later.

visuals.quote: the mud mosque in Timbuktu today

scenes.say: While Musa was away, his general had taken the city of Gao, on the Niger River. Musa visited it on his way home, and a mosque was built there too. His empire was now at its largest.
He also sent young scholars from Mali to study in Fez, in Morocco, so they could come back as teachers. He was not only buying buildings. He was buying knowledge.

Around it grew schools and libraries. Timbuktu became one of the great centers of learning in the Islamic world. Scholars copied books on law, astronomy and medicine. Families hid those manuscripts for centuries.
And Europe noticed. Fifty years later, a map made in Majorca showed an African king on a throne, holding a gold nugget. That king is Musa.

scenes.say: Musa died around thirteen thirty seven. And the empire he made famous began to come apart.

His son Maghan ruled only a few years. Then Musa's brother, Sulayman, took the throne. And in thirteen fifty two, the most famous traveler of the medieval world arrived to see Mali for himself. Ibn Battuta.

He praised the safety of the roads. A traveler, he wrote, had nothing to fear from thieves. But he complained that the new king was stingy. His welcome gift was some bread, some beef and yogurt. Musa's generosity, it seems, had not been passed down.

visuals.text: There is complete security in their country. Neither traveler nor inhabitant has anything to fear.

scenes.say: Rival princes fought over the throne. Provinces broke away. In fourteen sixty eight, the rising Songhai Empire took Timbuktu.

And those Europeans who saw the gold on the map? They came. Not across the desert, but by sea. And within two centuries, the trade that made Mali rich had moved to the coast... where a new trade, in human beings, would grow into one of the darkest chapters in history.
And the books of Timbuktu? Their story is not over either. In twenty twelve, armed militants took over the city. They destroyed ancient tombs of saints. And the manuscripts were in danger.

So the librarians of Timbuktu did something incredible. Quietly, box by box, they smuggled hundreds of thousands of manuscripts out of the city, on donkey carts, in cars and on boats down the Niger. When the militants retreated in twenty thirteen, they set fire to a library. Some manuscripts burned. But most of them had already been saved.
Seven hundred years later, the most valuable thing Musa brought home was not the gold. It was the books. And people risked their lives to save them.
That is the part the legend never tells. Gold can make a king famous. It can't keep an empire alive. And the wealth everyone wanted to find... changed who was being traded.
So, was he really the richest man who ever lived? You may have seen the number. Four hundred billion dollars.

visuals.label: the number online
visuals.note: a modern guess, not a historical figure

scenes.say: The honest answer is that nobody can calculate it. There were no bank records, and he controlled a share of the gold of half a continent. His wealth was so big that the people who wrote about him didn't have words for it.
But we can measure it another way. Seven hundred years later, a city on the other side of the desert still remembered the year a stranger made their gold worthless.
Three things this story teaches. One. Wealth tied to a single person rarely outlives him.
Two. Owning the road can be worth more than owning the mine. And three. Flood a market with anything, even gold, and you make it worth less.

lines: 2. Own the road, not the mine.
3. Flood a market, it loses value.

scenes.say: I'm your narrator, and this has been the story of Mansa Musa. If you want the next dark chapter of history the textbooks skipped... you know where the button is.
